Endogenous Buyer Participation The analysis so far treats buyers as captive. The platform maximizes aggregate seller profit, \Pi(\lambda_H,\lambda_L), while a fixed unit mass of buyers receives a fixed attention budget \Lambda. This benchmark isolates the rent-preservation motive. It also shuts down the buyer-side discipline that is central in many platform markets: if buyers can leave, the platform must care about the surplus its ranking or recommendation system delivers to them.
This buyer-side discipline is the organizing force of two-sided-market theory: a platform that monetizes one side must still compete for participation on the other, and it protects — or even subsidizes — whichever side is more willing to walk away, because attracting that side is what makes the paying side valuable. What differs here is the instrument. The platform in our setting sets no buyer-side price; its only lever is the allocation of attention across sellers. The same force therefore operates through the recommendation feed rather than through a fee: improving the feed is worthwhile only insofar as it draws in buyers and thereby enlarges the seller rents the platform extracts. Allowing the number of buyers to be elastic is therefore useful for assessing to what extent the distortion discussed in the previous section depends on buyers being unable to leave.
This section introduces that discipline in the simplest possible way. The platform still does not charge buyers, still earns revenue from the seller side, and still chooses the per-buyer meeting rates (\lambda_H,\lambda_L), with \lambda_H+\lambda_L=\Lambda. The only change is that the mass of buyers who join the platform depends on the buyer surplus generated by the platform's attention allocation. Higher buyer surplus attracts more buyers; more buyers increase the seller rents from which the platform earns revenue. Buyer participation therefore pushes the platform away from pure seller-rent maximization and toward buyer-surplus maximization.
There is a unit mass of potential buyers. A buyer's outside option u_{a} is drawn from a distribution with c.d.f. G and density g=G' and elasticity \varepsilon_G(U):= U g(U)/G(U). A buyer joins the platform if and only if her platform surplus exceeds her outside option: U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\ge u_{a}, where U_\Lambda(\lambda_H) \equiv U(\lambda_H,\lambda_L) is per-buyer buyer surplus in the induced price-posting equilibrium and is given by equation (18). Thus the active buyer mass is G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)). We assume that G is continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, and strictly positive on the range of U_\Lambda(\lambda_H) induced by feasible attention allocations.
The per-buyer price-posting equilibrium is unchanged by this participation margin. Each active buyer receives the same meeting rates as before, and the platform extracts a common share \beta of seller profits. Since \beta is common across seller types, it does not enter sellers' price-posting problem. With active buyer mass G(U), aggregate seller profit is G(U)\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H), where \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H) \equiv \Pi(\lambda_H,\lambda_L) is given by equation (22). Finally, platform revenue is \beta G(U)\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H). Free entry simply scales seller masses: n_j c_j = (1-\beta)G(U)\lambda_j\bar\pi_j, j\in\{H,L\}. Thus participation changes the size of the market, but not the per-buyer objects U and \Pi.
Planner's solution The planner benchmark is unchanged by endogenous participation when platform extraction is removed. With \beta=0, aggregate welfare is \mathcal W(\lambda_H) = G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H))U_\Lambda(\lambda_H) + \int_{U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)}^\infty \omega\,dG(\omega). Differentiating gives \frac{d\mathcal W}{d\lambda_H} = G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H))U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H). Thus the planner still maximizes per-buyer buyer surplus U_\Lambda. The planner's solution is again given by Propositions 1 and 2.
Platform's solution Denote the platform's optimal choice with endogenous buyer entry by \lambda_H^E. Since platform revenue is \beta G(U)\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H), dropping the constant \beta, \lambda_H^E solves \max_{\lambda_H\in[0,\Lambda]} \Omega(\lambda_H) \equiv G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H))\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H). Throughout this section we maintain Assumption 1 and assume that the planner's corner comparison favors the all-H corner:
\frac{z_H}{z_L} \ge r(\Lambda), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad U_\Lambda(\Lambda) \ge U_\Lambda(0),
where r(\Lambda)=\mathcal P(\Lambda)/\mathcal P(\Lambda x) is the corner ratio of Lemma 2. Condition (33) says that buyers weakly prefer the all-H allocation to the all-L allocation; by Proposition 2, the planner's solution is then the all-H corner, \lambda_H^P=\Lambda, uniquely so when the inequality is strict. Since r(\Lambda) is strictly decreasing, (33) is a budget threshold: it holds if and only if \Lambda\ge\bar\Lambda, where r(\bar\Lambda)=z_H/z_L, with \bar\Lambda=0 if and only if x^2 z_H\ge z_L. The condition x^2 z_H\ge z_L of Proposition 2 is thus the special case in which (33) holds for every budget. Proposition 5 below shows that, under (33), buyer participation always pushes the platform toward more high-quality exposure. The condition cannot be dropped.If z_H/z_L is below r(Lambda), then U at the all-H corner is below U at the all-L corner and, since U is U-shaped, lambda_H = 0 is the unique maximizer of buyer surplus. For outside-option distributions with constant participation elasticity M, a sufficiently participation-sensitive platform abandons rent maximization downward, toward the all-L corner that buyers prefer, and the endogenous optimum falls below 1/x as M grows large.
The case \Lambda\le1/x is immediate. In this case the all-H allocation maximizes both buyer surplus—by Proposition 1 and condition (33)—and aggregate seller profit, by Lemma 3. Endogenous buyer participation therefore cannot change the platform's choice, and \lambda_H^E=\Lambda.
We therefore focus on \Lambda\gt 1/x. Let \lambda_H^* denote the captive-buyer platform optimum characterized in Proposition 3. In this region, the captive-buyer platform optimum is interior and lies beyond the rent-maximizing scale 1/x, but remains close to it because further high-quality exposure dissipates seller rents. Endogenous buyer participation changes the platform's objective by making buyer surplus matter directly: the platform now maximizes G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H))\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H), rather than \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H) alone. Under condition (33), the interval [\lambda_H^*,\Lambda] is precisely the path from the captive-buyer optimum to the planner's allocation. The next lemma compares allocations that deliver the same buyer surplus, which is the relevant comparison for our analysis.
LEMMA 4. Fix \Lambda\gt 0 and 0\le\lambda_H\lt \lambda_H'\le\Lambda. If U_\Lambda(\lambda_H')=U_\Lambda(\lambda_H), then \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H')\gt \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H). Since net buyer surplus is gross surplus minus dissipated seller rents, U_\Lambda=S_\Lambda-\Pi_\Lambda. Hence \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H')-\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H)=S_\Lambda(\lambda_H')-S_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\gt 0 by Lemma 1.
Among allocations that deliver the same buyer surplus, the one with more high-quality exposure carries strictly higher seller rents: gross surplus rises with \lambda_H, and with buyer surplus held fixed the entire gain accrues to sellers. The lemma lets us compare allocations across the two branches of the U-shaped buyer surplus without comparing the corners directly.
We now show that, under condition (33), \lambda_H^E\gt \lambda_H^*: a platform facing endogenous buyer entry exposes buyers to more high-quality sellers than the captive-buyer benchmark. By Proposition 3, \Pi_\Lambda is single-peaked: strictly increasing on [0,\lambda_H^*], with maximizer \lambda_H^*\gt 1/x, and strictly decreasing thereafter. By Proposition 1, U_\Lambda is U-shaped, falling to a unique trough and then rising. The trough lies strictly to the left of 1/x: by equation (20), U_\Lambda'\left(\frac1x\right) = (1-x)z_L e^{-(1+\lambda_L)}\left[R e^{\lambda_L}-(1+\lambda_L)\right]\gt 0, since R\gt 1 and e^{\lambda_L}\ge 1+\lambda_L, where \lambda_L=\Lambda-1/x. Hence U_\Lambda is strictly increasing throughout the region [1/x,\Lambda]. Note that this step uses only the maintained assumption x z_H\gt z_L.
These facts rule out any optimum at or below \lambda_H^*. First, consider \lambda_H\lt 1/x. If U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\le U_\Lambda(1/x), moving to 1/x weakly raises buyer surplus and strictly raises seller profit (as \Pi_\Lambda is increasing on [0,1/x]), and therefore strictly raises the platform's objective \Omega. If instead U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\gt U_\Lambda(1/x), then \lambda_H must lie on the decreasing branch of U_\Lambda, so U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\le U_\Lambda(0)\le U_\Lambda(\Lambda), where the second inequality is condition (33). Since U_\Lambda increases continuously from U_\Lambda(1/x)\lt U_\Lambda(\lambda_H) to U_\Lambda(\Lambda)\ge U_\Lambda(\lambda_H) on [1/x,\Lambda], there is a unique \lambda_H'\in(1/x,\Lambda] with U_\Lambda(\lambda_H')=U_\Lambda(\lambda_H): the allocation on the rising branch that delivers the same buyer surplus. By Lemma 4, \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H')\gt \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H), and therefore \Omega(\lambda_H')\gt \Omega(\lambda_H). In either case, no allocation below 1/x can be optimal. Second, on [1/x,\lambda_H^*] both \Pi_\Lambda and U_\Lambda are strictly increasing, so \Omega is strictly increasing and the platform never stops before \lambda_H^*. Finally, at \lambda_H^* the seller-rent motive is exhausted, \Pi_\Lambda'(\lambda_H^*)=0, yet buyer surplus is still strictly rising, U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H^*)\gt 0, so the platform's objective \Omega is still strictly increasing at \lambda_H^*, so the platform strictly prefers to move beyond it.To see this formally, note that the derivative of Omega at the captive optimum equals G times the (zero) rent derivative plus g times the (positive) surplus derivative times Pi, which is strictly positive. Every platform optimum therefore satisfies \lambda_H^E\gt \lambda_H^*, establishing the following proposition.
PROPOSITION 5. Suppose Assumption 1 holds, \Lambda\gt 1/x, and z_H/z_L\ge r(\Lambda). Then every platform optimum satisfies \lambda_H^E \gt \lambda_H^*. Thus any positive buyer-side responsiveness makes the platform allocate more attention to high-quality sellers than in the captive-buyer benchmark. See the discussion above.
The captive platform stops where the marginal seller rent vanishes, whereas the entry-responsive platform internalizes a further margin: extra high-quality exposure raises buyer surplus, draws in more buyers, and a larger buyer base lifts total rents, which is a first-order gain the captive benchmark ignores.
The platform's first-order condition highlights these forces. At an interior optimum the elasticity of the objective with respect to high-quality exposure vanishes, which can be decomposed into the platform's two motives:
\lambda_H\frac{\Omega'(\lambda_H)}{\Omega(\lambda_H)} = \lambda_H\frac{\Pi_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)}{\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H)} + \varepsilon_G\big(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\big)\lambda_H\frac{U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)}{U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)},
where the first term is the seller-rent elasticity and the second combines the buyer-participation elasticity \varepsilon_G with the buyer-surplus elasticity. The first term is the seller-rent motive of the baseline model. The second is the buyer-attraction motive: by the chain rule it is precisely the elasticity of the active buyer mass G(U_\Lambda) with respect to exposure, the product of how strongly surplus responds to exposure, \lambda_H U_\Lambda'/U_\Lambda, and how strongly participation responds to surplus, \varepsilon_G. The platform therefore internalizes buyer surplus only through \varepsilon_G: when participation is fixed, \varepsilon_G\equiv 0, the second term drops out and the condition collapses to the baseline \Pi_\Lambda'=0. At the captive optimum \lambda_H^* the seller-rent elasticity is already zero while the buyer-surplus elasticity is strictly positive, so the objective elasticity is strictly positive and the platform gains by exposing buyers to more high-quality sellers. The size of this buyer-attraction term—and hence of the departure from rent maximization—scales one-for-one with \varepsilon_G.
On the relevant interval \lambda_H \in (\lambda_H^*,\Lambda], buyer surplus is increasing and seller rent is decreasing: U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)\gt 0, since U_\Lambda is strictly increasing on [1/x,\Lambda] as shown above, and \Pi_\Lambda'(\lambda_H) \lt 0 by Proposition 3. Hence the first-order condition in (34) can be written as an elasticity comparison:
\frac{\varepsilon_{\Omega}(\lambda_H)}{\varepsilon_{U}(\lambda_H)} = \varepsilon_G\big(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)\big) - \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H), \qquad \lambda_H\in (\lambda_H^*,\Lambda],
where \varepsilon_{\Omega}(\lambda_H), \varepsilon_U(\lambda_H), \varepsilon_\Pi(\lambda_H), and \varepsilon_G(U) denote the elasticities of \Omega(\lambda_H), U_\Lambda(\lambda_H), \Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H), and G(U), respectively. Furthermore, \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H) is defined by
\eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H) := -\frac{\varepsilon_{\Pi}(\lambda_H)}{\varepsilon_{U}(\lambda_H)} = - \frac{\Pi_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)}{\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda_H)} \frac{U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)}{U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)}, \qquad \lambda_H\in (\lambda_H^*,\Lambda].
The object \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H) has a simple economic interpretation. It is the buyer-participation elasticity required to make the platform willing to choose \lambda_H. Moving further toward H raises buyer surplus but reduces seller rents. The term -\varepsilon_\Pi(\lambda_H) measures the percentage seller-rent loss from increasing high-quality exposure, while \varepsilon_U(\lambda_H) measures the percentage gain in buyer surplus. Their ratio is therefore the elasticity of buyer participation needed to offset the rent loss. Thus \eta_\Lambda is the platform-side cost of improving the ranking, measured in units of buyer responsiveness.
The next lemma is the key technical step. It shows that this economically meaningful hurdle becomes strictly harder to clear as the platform moves from the captive-buyer allocation toward the planner allocation. This monotonicity is not immediate. The object \eta_\Lambda combines rent levels, marginal rent losses, buyer-surplus levels, and marginal buyer-surplus gains, all generated by the Burdett–Judd kernels at two different meeting rates. Showing that these terms collapse into a monotone hurdle is the main technical contribution of this part of the analysis.
LEMMA 5. Suppose Assumption 1 holds and \Lambda\gt 1/x. Then \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H), defined in (36), is strictly increasing on [\lambda_H^*,\Lambda]. See Appendix A.7.
Lemma 5 turns the endogenous-entry problem into a simple elasticity comparison. The left-hand side of the interior condition, \varepsilon_G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)), comes from the buyer side: it is determined by how sensitive buyer participation is to delivered surplus. The right-hand side, \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H), comes from the platform side: it is determined by the primitives x,z_H,z_L,\Lambda and by the Burdett–Judd rent kernel. Since U_\Lambda is increasing on [\lambda_H^*,\Lambda], a decreasing surplus elasticity makes \varepsilon_G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H)) weakly decreasing in \lambda_H. By Lemma 5, the hurdle \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H) is strictly increasing. Hence the two sides can cross at most once.
ASSUMPTION 2. The buyer-participation elasticity \varepsilon_G(U) is weakly decreasing for all U\in[U_\Lambda(\lambda_H^*),U_\Lambda(\Lambda)].
This is a shape restriction on buyer entry, not on the matching technology. It requires buyer participation to become no more elastic as delivered surplus rises. Constant-elasticity functions satisfy it with equality.
PROPOSITION 6. Suppose Assumption 1 holds, \Lambda\gt 1/x, z_H/z_L\ge r(\Lambda), and Assumption 2. Then the platform's optimal \lambda_H^E is uniquely determined by the first-order condition (35) with complementary slackness. In particular, if the optimum is interior, it is the unique solution of \varepsilon_G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H^E)) = \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H^E). The optimum is the upper corner, \lambda_H^E=\Lambda, if and only if \varepsilon_G(U_\Lambda(\Lambda)) \ge \eta_\Lambda(\Lambda). See Appendix A.8.
The proposition gives a primitive version of the buyer-discipline result. After the captive-buyer optimum, more high-quality exposure raises buyer surplus but lowers seller rents. The platform continues increasing \lambda_H only when buyer participation is elastic enough to compensate for the rent loss. The required elasticity is precisely \eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H). Under Assumption 1, this hurdle rises as the platform moves toward the planner allocation. Under Assumption 2, buyer participation does not become more responsive as surplus rises. Together, these two forces imply a single crossing and make the first-order condition globally valid.
The economic message is that platform degradation depends on how easy it is to lose buyers. The elasticity \varepsilon_G measures the size of the marginal buyer pool relative to the active buyer mass. If \varepsilon_G is small, improving recommendations attracts few new buyers, and worsening recommendations drives few buyers away, for example because of switching costs or network externalities. The platform then behaves close to the captive-buyer benchmark and mainly protects seller rents. If \varepsilon_G is large, improving recommendations attracts many buyers, for example because competing platforms are close substitutes, so the platform puts more weight on buyer surplus. Once this elasticity is high enough throughout the relevant range, buyer participation fully disciplines the platform and the optimum is the planner's all-H allocation. Thus platform degradation is most severe when users are captive and disappears when users can easily switch. Finally, note that one force that we ignored here is that many platforms spend resources to keep \varepsilon_G low in order to capture buyers.One channel is that platforms may take actions that reduce buyer-participation elasticity by making users less likely to switch or by limiting third-party tools that facilitate switching. These actions can include acquisitions of close or emerging substitutes, such as Meta's acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp, Google's acquisition of YouTube, or Amazon's acquisition of Quidsi/Diapers.com, as well as interoperability restrictions. A recent example of the latter is Meta's 2022 cutoff of the OG App's access to Instagram's social-graph data; the app had marketed itself as an algorithm-free, chronological alternative to Instagram. We do not model these strategies. The point is that they can lower buyer responsiveness and move the platform's attention allocation toward the captive-buyer benchmark.
Conclusion This paper studies how a seller-funded platform allocates scarce buyer attention. The platform does not set retail prices, but chooses which sellers buyers are likely to meet. Sellers then compete by posting prices, and the platform extracts a share of seller profits. This distinction between price control and attention control matters: even when sellers price competitively, the platform can distort market outcomes by choosing the competitive environment in which those prices are set.
The central mechanism is rent preservation. Buyer welfare is created when a buyer has multiple effective offers and sellers compete for the sale. Platform revenue, by contrast, is tied to seller rents, which are highest when a buyer has exactly one effective offer. Under the clean condition x^2 z_H\ge z_L, the planner allocates all attention to high-quality sellers, while the platform expands high-quality exposure only until the effective meeting rate is near its rent-maximizing scale. Beyond that point, the platform routes additional attention toward the low-quality mass-market side. The buyer-surplus loss therefore combines an allocative loss from too little high-quality exposure with an excess-rent loss from seller/platform rents paid by buyers. The analysis suggests that the welfare effects of platform search depend not only on how much buyers can search, but also on who controls the resulting attention. Better search capacity need not move the allocation closer to the social benchmark when the platform monetizes seller rents.
The calibration of Section 3.4 suggests this distortion is not a knife-edge concern. Using publicly available relevance data for Amazon product search and Google passage ranking, we find that the compositional distortion identified by the model is substantial.
The platform's under-allocation of high-quality exposure connects formally to what Doctorow (2022) terms enshittification: the observed tendency of digital platforms to progressively degrade the user experience in order to extract surplus from business customers (sellers). In Doctorow's account, platforms first win users by being genuinely useful, then pivot allocation toward sellers once user lock-in is sufficient. The present paper identifies a static mechanism that produces the same degradation without any deliberate long-run strategy, and our calibration indicates that both Amazon and Google satisfy the conditions for over-recommending standardized products. Doctorow predicted that the platforms ultimately die out. Our model provides no indication that this is necessarily the case, although a full analysis would require extension to a dynamic setup. We view this as a promising avenue for future research.

By Proposition 3 the platform's allocation is the unique interior root of the reduced first-order condition, which, after substituting \lambda_H^*=\Lambda-\lambda_L^*, is equivalent to equation (A1). As shown in the proof of Proposition 3, the derivative d\Lambda/d\lambda_L^* is given by (A2) and is strictly positive, so \lambda_L^* is strictly increasing in \Lambda with d\lambda_L^*/d\Lambda=\bigl(d\Lambda/d\lambda_L^*\bigr)^{-1}. To establish the hump shape of \lambda_L^*(\Lambda), recall from the proof of Proposition 3 that d^2\Lambda/d(\lambda_L^*)^2, given in (A3), is first negative and then positive, with the sign change occurring at \lambda^c. Because d\Lambda/d\lambda_L^*\gt 0, the inverse-function rule gives \frac{d}{d\Lambda}\left(\frac{d\lambda_L^*}{d\Lambda}\right) = -\frac{d^2\Lambda/d(\lambda_L^*)^2}{\left(d\Lambda/d\lambda_L^*\right)^3}. Since d\Lambda/d\lambda_L^*\gt 0, this implies d\lambda_L^*/d\Lambda \gt 1 whenever \lambda_L^*\gt 1, hence for all sufficiently large \Lambda. The convergence to 1 is therefore from above.

A.8 Proof of Proposition 6 By Proposition 5, every platform optimum satisfies \lambda_H\gt \lambda_H^*, so it suffices to consider \lambda_H\in(\lambda_H^*,\Lambda]. Throughout this interval U_\Lambda'(\lambda_H)\gt 0, hence \varepsilon_U(\lambda_H)\gt 0, and equation (35) then implies that \varepsilon_{\Omega}(\lambda_H), equivalently \Omega'(\lambda_H), has the same sign as \varepsilon_G(U_\Lambda(\lambda_H))-\eta_\Lambda(\lambda_H).
